prompt: Which of these is allocated once, when the server starts, and shared by every process?
hint: Look at which one is a postmaster parameter.

choices.text: work_mem
choices.why: Taken per sort or hash, inside one process, and given back afterwards.

choices.text: maintenance_work_mem
choices.why: Taken by one maintenance operation in one process.

choices.text: shared_buffers
choices.why: Right. 128 MB by default, sized at start and kept until the server stops.

choices.text: temp_buffers
choices.why: A session's own cache for its temporary tables.

prompt: `shared_memory_size` is 143 MB while `shared_buffers` is 128 MB. What is the difference?
hint: The shared segment holds more than pages.

choices.text: The work_mem of the connections open at the moment
choices.why: work_mem is private to each process and is not part of the shared segment.

choices.text: Lock tables, WAL buffers and other bookkeeping
choices.why: Right. The buffers are most of the segment, not all of it.

choices.text: The operating system's page cache for the data files
choices.why: That belongs to the kernel and is counted in buff/cache, not by PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Rounding: 128 MB is shown in binary and 143 in decimal units
choices.why: Both are in the same unit; 15 MB is real memory.

prompt: Match each parameter to what it is.
hint: Shared, private, maintenance, or no memory at all.

pairs.right: one cache of pages for every process
the ceiling for one sort or hash
the ceiling for one index build or vacuum
an estimate for the planner, allocating nothing

prompt: With `shared_buffers` at 128 MB, a parallel `count(*)` read all 8334 pages of `orders`. How many of them were in the cache afterwards?
hint: Three processes, a ring of 32 each.

prompt: Why did a 65 MB table not stay in a 128 MB cache after being read in full?
hint: Compare the table with a quarter of the cache.

choices.text: The cache was already full of system catalogues
choices.why: 16127 of 16384 buffers were unused after the restart.

choices.text: count(*) reads the index instead of the table
choices.why: The plan said Parallel Seq Scan on orders, 8334 pages read.

choices.text: The pages were evicted as soon as the query ended
choices.why: Nothing evicts pages at the end of a query; with 1 GB of cache all 8334 stayed.

choices.text: A big sequential scan gets a small ring of buffers
choices.why: Right. Larger than a quarter of shared_buffers, so 32 buffers per process, to protect other tables' pages.

prompt: `Buffers: shared read=8238` and yet the query took a fraction of a second. Where did the 8238 pages come from?
hint: read means not in shared_buffers. It does not say from where.

choices.text: From the disk, which is very fast on this machine
choices.why: They never reached the disk: the kernel had them cached.

choices.text: From another backend's private memory
choices.why: Backends do not share private memory; shared pages live in shared_buffers.

choices.text: The operating system's page cache
choices.why: Right. The second cache under PostgreSQL's own; a read there is a copy in memory.

choices.text: From the write-ahead log
choices.why: The WAL is read in recovery, not to answer queries.

prompt: Why does the usual advice start shared_buffers at about a quarter of memory rather than most of it?
hint: There is a second cache.

choices.text: The kernel's page cache needs memory too, and holds much of the same data
choices.why: Right. Memory given to one cache is taken from the other, and processes need private memory as well.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses values above 25%
choices.why: It accepts far more; 25% is advice, not a limit.

choices.text: Larger caches make every query slower
choices.why: The documentation says above 40% rarely helps, not that it harms every query.

choices.text: Linux limits shared memory to a quarter of RAM
choices.why: No such limit stopped 1 GB here; the rule comes from the double caching.

prompt: In EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which line says a sort spilled to temporary files?
hint: Look at the Sort Method.

choices.text: Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 63639kB
choices.why: That sort fitted in memory, with work_mem at 100MB.

choices.text: Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 25kB
choices.why: A sort that kept only five rows, in memory.

choices.text: Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 21632kB
choices.why: Right. Sorted in pieces, written to disk, merged.

choices.text: Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 4881kB
choices.why: A hash in one batch fitted; more batches would mean a spill.

prompt: The HashAggregate used 4881 kB in a single batch with `work_mem` at 4 MB. How did it fit?
hint: One multiplier applies to hashes only.

choices.text: work_mem is per query, and the sort above used only 25 kB
choices.why: Each step has its own allowance; nothing is shared between them.

choices.text: hash_mem_multiplier is 2, so a hash gets 8 MB
choices.why: Right. Hashes cost more to spill, so they get twice the allowance.

choices.text: The limit is checked only at the end of the operation
choices.why: A sort over the limit spilled while running; the hash simply had a larger limit.

choices.text: 4881 kB is less than 4 MB in binary units
choices.why: 4 MB is 4096 kB; 4881 is more.

prompt: To give one session room for a big sort without changing anybody else, run ___ work_mem = '100MB'; in that session.
hint: The SQL command for a session's own value.

prompt: The sort spilled 21632 kB to disk with 4 MB, yet did not fit until work_mem was well above 21 MB. Why?
hint: Compare what a row costs on disk and in memory.

choices.text: The temporary files are compressed
choices.why: They are not compressed; they are just more compact than the in-memory form.

choices.text: In memory each row carries pointers and headers
choices.why: Right. The in-memory sort took 63639 kB, about three times the files.

choices.text: The parallel workers each needed a copy of the rows
choices.why: This plan had no Gather: one process did the sort.

choices.text: work_mem is counted in 8 kB pages, not kilobytes
choices.why: pg_settings gave its unit as kB.

prompt: Which of these uses maintenance_work_mem rather than work_mem?
hint: Not a query.

choices.text: SELECT … ORDER BY
choices.why: A query's sort uses work_mem.

choices.text: SELECT … GROUP BY
choices.why: A HashAggregate uses work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier.

choices.text: A hash join
choices.why: Also a query step, also work_mem.

choices.text: CREATE INDEX
choices.why: Right, along with VACUUM and adding a foreign key.

prompt: The build at 1 MB wrote a 20070400-byte temporary file; the build at 64 MB wrote none. Both took about half a second. What does that show?
hint: Where did the 19 MB go?

choices.text: maintenance_work_mem has no effect on CREATE INDEX
choices.why: It decided whether the sort spilled: a file at 1 MB, none at 64 MB.

choices.text: The second build reused the first one's sorted file
choices.why: The file is deleted when the operation ends, and the index was dropped.

choices.text: Index builds always run in parallel, hiding the cost
choices.why: max_parallel_maintenance_workers was 0: one process each time.

choices.text: Spilling is cheap while the file stays in the page cache
choices.why: Right. On a machine where it reaches the disk, the gap grows.

prompt: maintenance_work_mem is 1GB on a 4 GB machine. Three autovacuum workers run while somebody builds an index. How much memory may those four take?
hint: autovacuum_work_mem is -1. And vacuum has a cap of its own in 16.

choices.text: 1 GB, shared among the four
choices.why: It is per operation: each worker and the build get their own.

choices.text: 64 MB each, because autovacuum ignores maintenance_work_mem
choices.why: -1 means autovacuum uses maintenance_work_mem.

choices.text: Only the index build, since autovacuum pauses during it
choices.why: Autovacuum works on other tables at the same time.

choices.text: Up to 4 GB: each takes its own
choices.why: Right. Vacuum caps at 1 GB, and so does this setting: four allowances, the whole machine.

prompt: `SET effective_cache_size = '1TB'` was accepted on a 15 GB machine. What did it change?
hint: It allocates nothing.

choices.text: It reserved a terabyte of swap for the session
choices.why: free showed no swap, and the parameter allocates nothing.

choices.text: It enlarged shared_buffers for this session
choices.why: shared_buffers is postmaster: no session can change it.

choices.text: The planner's estimate of what is cached
choices.why: Right. It is a belief the planner uses for index costs, nothing more.

choices.text: Nothing, because the value exceeds the memory
choices.why: It took effect for the session; SHOW printed 1TB. It just is not true.

prompt: A 4 GB machine: shared_buffers 1024 MB, 512 MB for the system, 1024 MB of page cache kept, 100 connections with two operations each. What work_mem, in MB, does the course's arithmetic give, rounded to a whole number?
A query with two hash joins and a sort runs with two parallel helpers. How many times work_mem may it use, at most, by the course's count?
hint: Three processes; a hash counts twice.

prompt: A backend is killed by Linux's out-of-memory killer. What does the postmaster do?
hint: It cannot trust shared memory any more.

choices.text: Ends every connection and restarts
choices.why: Right. One runaway query becomes an outage for everybody.

choices.text: Starts a replacement for that one backend and carries on
choices.why: A killed process may have left shared memory inconsistent, so all go.

choices.text: Lowers work_mem automatically for every session
choices.why: The server changes no setting by itself.

choices.text: Nothing; the client sees an error and reconnects
choices.why: Every other client sees an error too, because they are all disconnected.

prompt: A dashboard opens the same 120 MB report twenty times at once on the 4 GB virtual machine with work_mem 8MB. What runs out first?
hint: 20 × 120 MB, against the 1536 MB share.

choices.text: shared_buffers, which the reports fill with their sorts
choices.why: Sorts use private memory; shared_buffers stays 1 GB whatever they do.

choices.text: max_connections, at twenty
choices.why: max_connections is 100; twenty connections are well inside it.

choices.text: Nothing: work_mem caps the total at 8 MB per connection
choices.why: It caps each step, never a connection's total.

choices.text: The page cache, then free memory
choices.why: Right. 2400 MB is more than the share for sorts and hashes; the kernel gives up cache first.

prompt: Put the steps of the course's memory budget in order.
hint: Shared cache first, the division last.
items: give shared_buffers a quarter of memory
set aside memory for the system and processes
keep a quarter for the page cache
divide what is left by connections × operations
trap: Dividing before the shares are taken out sizes work_mem against memory that is already spoken for.

prompt: After raising shared_buffers from 128 MB to 1 GB, the second count of orders went from read=8238 to hit=8334, and the time barely changed. What explains that?
hint: Where were the pages before?

choices.text: The page cache already served the misses
choices.why: Right. On a machine whose data does not fit in memory, the hits would save real reads.

choices.text: The extra memory went to work_mem instead
choices.why: shared_buffers and work_mem are separate; the restart grew only the shared segment.

choices.text: A count reads no pages, so the cache is irrelevant
choices.why: It read all 8334 pages, as the Buffers line shows.

choices.text: The parallel workers bypass shared_buffers
choices.why: They read through it: hit=8334 counts their pages too.

prompt: Match each value of the course's budget for the 15 GB recording machine.
hint: A quarter, the division, three quarters, four allowances.
